explanation: "Not as good as" is the correct positive-degree equivalent of "better"; option (c) reverses the meaning (claims begging is better) and (d) misuses the superlative "best...than".
The comparative-to-positive pattern for a superlative is "No other X is as [adjective] as Y"; the other options misuse "fast than" without "as" or "more".
Superlative "costliest" converts to "No metal is as costly as gold," the standard positive-degree equivalence.
"Work" is uncountable, so the interrogative needs "much," not "many" — a classic countable/uncountable trap in options (b) and (d).
An exclamatory sentence with "What a...!" converts to a plain assertive statement of the same fact: "The rose is a beautiful flower."
"Nobody will deny X" converts to the affirmative "Everybody will admit X" — the double negative (deny + nobody) becomes a straightforward affirmation.
A gerund phrase ("his being elected") becomes a finite noun clause in the complex form: "that he had been elected," using past perfect since the election preceded the declaring.
The adjective "pleasant" becomes an adjective clause "where it was pleasant"; the tense must stay past ("was") to match "reached," ruling out the present-tense options.
"Loss" (noun) fits after "the ___ of his watch"; "lost/lose/loose" are not nouns that fit this slot.
An action starting in the past and continuing to now ("since this morning") takes the present perfect continuous, "have been waiting."
A daily habitual action takes simple present: "takes."
"While" introduces a simultaneous ongoing action, so the past/present continuous "is doing" fits the context of an interrupted action.
Present perfect "have finished" correctly pairs with the first-person subject "I" for a completed action with present relevance.
"When we reached" (simple past) signals an earlier completed action, so the service needed past perfect: "had already started."

Past perfect "had stolen" fits a narrative describing an action completed before another past reference point; "steal/steals" don't match past narration and "have stolen" doesn't agree with the singular subject "thief."
"Hurt" is both the past tense and past participle of "hurt" (an irregular unchanging verb), so it correctly follows "has."
"Sing" has the past participle "sung," required after "have you ever ___?" (present perfect).
One subject, one finite verb ("gave") with a participle phrase ("Finishing my paper") makes this a simple sentence, not a complex one.
"That the earth is round" is a noun clause (object of "knows"), making this a complex sentence.
"Which was black in colour" is a subordinate adjective clause, making the whole sentence complex.

"That he cannot stand" is best read as a noun clause (object of an implied verb, e.g., "[the fact] that he cannot stand [it]"); among the given options it fits noun clause best, though the fragment is oddly punctuated.

Correlative conjunctions like "either...or" traditionally join two elliptical independent clauses ("Either John has done it or Mary has done it"), so many grammar keys classify this as compound; note "Simple sentence" (the strictly modern-grammar answer) isn't offered among the options.
"Not only...but also" is the standard correlative conjunction joining two independent clauses into a compound sentence.

Only option (a) is a single clause (participial phrase + main clause), satisfying "to Simple"; the others keep two finite clauses (because/and) or two sentences. Note the participle technically dangles (grammatically modifying "nobody," not "he"), a known flaw in this drill's expected answer.
The second sentence becomes a noun clause object of "believe": "that he was cheating me," forming a complex sentence.
An appositive phrase ("Ram, my friend,") reduces the two sentences to one simple sentence.
"So...that" introduces a subordinate clause of result, correctly forming a complex sentence.
"Since" attaches as a subordinating conjunction directly to the reason clause: "I must be punished since I am at fault."
The relative pronoun "who" introduces the descriptive clause: "The woman who is in green saree is the manager of the team."
"Too...to" is the standard infinitive construction for this cause-effect pattern: "It is too cold to take a bath."
"Either John or Jacob has done it" correctly uses the correlative pair with singular verb agreement to the nearer subject.
"For" is used here as a coordinating conjunction meaning "because": "I cannot read his note-book for his hand writing is poor."
The adverb "successfully" is the concise adverbial rendering of "he wanted to succeed": "He tried to lift the box successfully."
"The movie being over" is the standard nominative absolute participial phrase for this sentence pair.
"Though" attached to the concession clause preserves the original logic: he failed despite working hard — "He failed though he worked hard."
The infinitive "to hear" expresses the cause of joy: "My father is overjoyed to hear of my success."
"Not only...but also" placed around the two adjectives correctly joins the pair: "She is not only beautiful, but also charming."
A plain declarative statement of fact is an affirmative sentence.
Punctuated and structured as a question, this is formally interrogative, even though it functions rhetorically to express disbelief.
A plain statement of fact with no special marking is assertive.
A direct command ("Fetch me...") is imperative.
A polite request/command beginning with "Please" is imperative.
The exclamatory "What a...!" converts to the plain declarative "It is a dreadful smell."
A statement converts to interrogative by inverting subject and auxiliary "does": "Does every rose have its thorn?"
The question converts to a plain statement of fact: "You have done your homework."
A polite modal question preserves the command's intent while being grammatically interrogative: "Can you please hurry up?"
The imperative form directly requests the action: "Close the door, please."
"Dotage" is the standard one-word substitute for foolish behaviour brought on by extreme old age.
"Archaeology" is the study of ancient societies through their material remains, the classic one-word substitution answer (distinct from anthropology, which studies humankind broadly).
"Give us the chance to do something" is the natural idiomatic collocation; "occasion" and "possibility" don't fit as smoothly in this context.
"Herd" is the correct collective noun for cows.
"Half" here modifies the adjective "dead" (indicating degree), so it functions as an adverb.
"Almost" modifies the adjective "ripe," indicating degree/extent, so it is an adverb of degree.
"Round" here indicates direction/position (bring the carriage around), making it an adverb of place — a classic Wren & Martin example.
"Shamefully" describes how the treatment was done, making it an adverb of manner.
"Not" negates the verb, making it an adverb of negation.
"Again" indicates repetition, making it an adverb of frequency.
Simple past "died" matches the simple past "was" in the same sentence; note options (a) and (d) are duplicate, defective "had died" entries.
"Up to now" signals present perfect: "have never managed"; the other options are either ungrammatical or use future tense incorrectly.
"Five minutes ago" is a definite past time marker requiring simple past: "went."
A habitual/routine fact ("twice weekly") takes simple present: "appears."
One subject, one finite verb, with only phrases (no subordinate clause) — a simple sentence.
"Or" is a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses, making this compound.
"What his address is" is a noun clause (object of "know"), making this complex.
"And" joins two independent clauses, making this compound.
"Besides being beautiful" is a prepositional/gerund phrase, not a clause, so the sentence remains simple.
"The sun having risen" is a nominative absolute (participial) phrase, not a finite clause, so this is a simple sentence.
"So" here joins two independent clauses as a coordinating conjunction, making this compound.
"So that" introduces a subordinate clause of purpose, making this complex.
"In spite of his poverty" is a prepositional phrase, not a clause, so the sentence is simple.
"That he cannot pay his fees" is a subordinate clause of result, making this complex.
A plain positive statement of fact is affirmative.
"As...as" signals the positive (equative) degree, not comparative.
"More...than" is the hallmark of the comparative degree.
"Not a poor man" is a negative construction (negates the adjective via "not").
"Most beautiful" marks the superlative degree.
"One of the greatest" uses the superlative form "greatest."
A plain declarative statement with no special marking is assertive.

This is a negative sentence ("No one..."), but "Negative" is not offered among the options; "Assertive," describing its declarative sentence-type, is the closest fit among Comparative/Assertive/Superlative/Positive.
"Not immortal" is a negative construction.
A plain positive statement with no negation is affirmative.
"That we will win the match" is a noun clause functioning as the object of "sure," not a modifier of a noun or verb.
"That has no turning" is an adjective clause modifying "lane."
"Where living was cheaper" is an adverb clause of place modifying "went."
"That the man was guilty" is a noun clause functioning as the object of "believed."
The idiomatic phrasing is "in need of an eye operation"; the underlined infinitive phrase is awkward and should be replaced with the prepositional noun phrase.
The correct idiom is "accustom yourself to" (not "with").
"Any able bodied man is" already agrees correctly (singular "any...man" with singular "is"), so no improvement is needed.
The idiomatic and grammatically correct phrasing is the possessive singular "your child's hand" (one hand held while walking, not "hands").
An unreal past conditional requires inversion of "had," not "have": "Had you not reached..."
The analogy is opposites: life is the opposite of death, so pleasure is to pain (its opposite).
"Parole" specifically refers to conditional early release, often tied to good behaviour.
"In course of time" is the idiomatic phrase for a gradual process over time.

"Literal translation" (staying close to the original wording) is the standard idiomatic collocation, more natural here than "verbatim," which usually describes exact quoted speech/text rather than translation.
"As blind as a bat" is the standard English simile idiom.
The young of an elephant is called a "calf."
This is the proverb "Beggars can't be choosers."
This reflects the proverb "No rose without a thorn," i.e., beauty conceals hidden pain — "thorn."
